analysis.one_liner: Bans the use of unregulated "soft money" to influence federal elections.
analysis.headline: The soft-money ban never left committee: it was referred to the House Oversight Committee on March 11, 1997, and received no further action before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal to spend money to influence any federal election unless that money followed the limits and reporting rules of federal campaign finance law — in other words, a ban on "soft money," the unlimited, largely unregulated donations that corporations, unions, and wealthy donors gave to political parties. In the 1990s, parties used soft money to pay for issue ads and campaign operations that indirectly helped their candidates. The bill was referred to the House Oversight Committee and never moved; no vote was ever held on it in the House or Senate, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary voters would have gained a campaign finance system in which money spent to influence federal elections had to comply with contribution limits and public disclosure rules, reducing the influence of six-figure corporate, union, and wealthy-donor donations funneled through the parties. Candidates of both parties would have had to fund campaigns through limited, disclosed contributions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting limited, disclosed campaign money

how_it_helps.text: The bill barred anyone from spending money to influence a federal campaign unless that money followed the limits, prohibitions, and reporting rules that already applied to regulated contributions under federal law, closing the loophole that allowed corporations, unions, and wealthy donors to give six-figure 'soft money' donations to the national parties.
It applied to elections after January 1997, so it would have governed federal races beginning immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Political parties would have lost the unlimited soft-money stream they used for issue advertising and party building; corporations, unions, and wealthy donors would have lost an unregulated channel for political influence, and would have had to operate under contribution limits and disclosure.

drawbacks.text: By forcing all federal-election spending into the regulated 'hard money' channel, the bill would have restricted how political parties could raise and spend money to support candidates, which critics argued limited party building and grassroots activity.
The ban applied to 'any person' spending funds to influence a federal campaign, raising free-speech objections that political expression could be pushed into more regulated, limited channels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — shutting down unlimited, unregulated soft-money spending in federal elections — was substantial and real, as later confirmed when Congress enacted a soft-money ban in 2002. The costs acknowledged by opponents were concerns about restricting party activity and free-spending rights, but for ordinary voters the bill carried little downside; its failure simply preserved the soft-money system until a later Congress acted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Oversight Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, so it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Representative Patsy Mink introduced the bill on March 11, 1997, with 13 cosponsors (12 Democrats and 1 Independent).
The House referred it the same day to the Committee on House Oversight, which took no further action on it.
Its only other activity was the sponsor's introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record on March 18, 1997.
No committee vote, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred, and the bill expired when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Parties, corporations, unions, and wealthy donors who wanted to keep giving and spending unlimited soft money in federal elections were better off because the bill died; voters who wanted limited, disclosed campaign money gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Parties and big donors to soft money

for.name: Rep. Patsy Mink
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban soft money in federal elections and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House schedule and the Oversight Committee's agenda; no campaign finance bill was brought to a floor vote in 1997, and the committee took no action on this bill.

against.name: House Committee on House Oversight
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, so support leaned Democratic, but the bill never advanced far enough for a partisan vote to record where each party stood.

industries.industry: Large donors, corporations, and unions giving soft money
industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to give unlimited, largely unregulated money to party committees to influence federal elections, forcing such spending into limited, disclosed channels.

industries.industry: Political parties and campaign fundraising operations
industries.note: Party committees would lose the soft-money revenue stream that had become a major source of national party financing.

industries.industry: Political advertising and campaign consulting industries
industries.note: Campaign spending channels would shift, but consultants and ad sellers would continue to be paid from regulated hard-money funds.
